newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians, still fearful, sift through rubble.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians, still fearful, sift through rubble.

text.p: Cambodian shopkeepers swept up debris in their capital on Tuesday but anguished that two days of fighting and a third of looting could not be easily brushed aside.
Troops loyal to powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen struggled to hoist a blasted-out tank on to a flatbed truck on the side of the main road from central Phnom Penh to the airport.
Ash from the ruins of nearby homes drifted across the road as young children hunted through the debris for scrap metal.
A dead soldier lay nearby, apparently left to rot because he was on the losing side.
Cambodia's coalition government, formed after U.N.-run elections in 1993, collapsed into violence on Saturday as forces loyal to the country's rival prime ministers went to war in the capital.
By Monday, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh had been ousted by Hun Sen.
At least 58 people were killed and as many as 200 others, mostly civilians, were wounded, in the three days of violence.
"This is a huge setback for the country, four years of hope and then this," said one businessman.

"It would take a very brave investor to even set a toe in Cambodia right now," said the businessman as he reeled off a list of top international companies that had suffered costly damage in the violence.
"God knows how much the violence will cost, I don't think anyone had war insurance," he said.
Most shops, schools, offices and banks remained closed on Tuesday as Cambodians gathered in small groups to try to make sense of the events of the past three days.
"This is a war, I'm afraid," said a middle-aged man who identified himself as Sophat. "I don't know what's going to happen," he said as he looked over a line of gutted shops on the airport road.
Ranariddh's forces fled their bases in and around the city on Sunday night but the turmoil was far from over.
Jubilant troops celebrated their victory with an orgy of looting and random violence.
The city's international airport as well as warehouses, shops, car showrooms and factories to the west of the city centre were completely stripped and gutted in the mayhem.
Four petrol stations on the airport road were destroyed by marauding soldiers. They even walked off with the petrol pump.
"If it was moveable, sadly it's been moved," said an official working with an international oil company.
As hundreds of foreigners scrambled to get on board Thai military evacuation flights on Tuesday, Cambodian children were playing in what little debris was left behind in the airport terminal.
The airport, only just renovated, was a scene of utter devastation after the fighting and looting.
Shellholes were blasted through the building walls. Visa forms, passport photos and broken glass carpeted the floor.
